Most likely not. The AS350B3 is part of the Ecureuil (AS350) family, not the Dauphin family (AS365, EC155, SA366, etc.). An AD on Dauphin-family servo-control nut torque inspections would normally be limited to Dauphin-type models (e.g., AS365 N3, EC155B/B1, and similar), so an AS350B3 would not be listed in its applicability. I have no document in front of me, so I cannot confirm the exact model list. Check the applicability section of the NPRM and the AD it would supersede. Also check whether a separate AS350-specific AD covers servo-control issues. Serial number 7890 and the normal category do not change this.

I can't confirm applicability. I have no document in front of me and don't recall the proposed AD's exact applicability paragraph or its Federal Register number. Being a normal-category Cabri G2 is probably necessary but may not be sufficient. Proposed ADs like this often limit applicability by serial number or by the ELT/antenna installation. Check the applicability section of the NPRM against your helicopter's data plate and logbooks, which give the serial number and installed ELT and antenna configuration. If the NPRM covers all Cabri G2 serial numbers, it applies to you. If it lists specific serial numbers or configurations, it applies only if yours matches.

I don't have the notice in front of me, so I can't confirm its applicability to your serial number or its compliance terms. What I can say generally: a proposed AD (NPRM) is not a final rule and is not legally binding. You are not required to comply with it, and it does not by itself ground your aircraft. An AD becomes mandatory only when the FAA publishes a final rule, and that rule sets the effective date and compliance times. Cessna 172 seat rail issues have been addressed before, notably in the 2008 AD 2009-02-05 and its related actions (Cessna SEB 07-?? / SIL). I can't confirm from memory which of those, if any, applies to your 2004 model year airplane. Before flying this weekend, please: (1) read the NPRM's applicability section to check whether your model and serial number 172S9876 are listed; (2) check whether any existing final AD on seat rails already applies to your aircraft and has been complied with, since those are binding now; (3) confirm with your A&P/IA and the aircraft maintenance records. If no final AD applies and nothing else makes the aircraft unairworthy, the NPRM alone doesn't ground you. I'd still do a seat-stop and rail inspection as a safety precaution, as a seat that slips on takeoff is dangerous.
